title: Why partials
text:
When you build a real web app with Jinja2, the same HTML fragments show up again and again: a video card, a badge, a pagination control, a row in a table. Copying the markup into every page works until the design changes and you have to find every copy. The fix in Python code is a function with explicit arguments. jinja_partials gives templates the same thing: a render_partial() global that renders a fragment file with exactly the data you pass it.
{% for v in videos %}
    {{ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v) }}
{% endfor %}
The fragment is an ordinary template file. It sees video and nothing else, so you can read its inputs at the call site, rename at the boundary (the loop variable v becomes video inside), and nest partials inside partials as deep as the design needs.

What is wrong with include and macro
Jinja already has two reuse mechanisms, and both fall short in a different way.
{% include %} hands the fragment the caller’s entire context. Nothing at the call site says what the fragment needs, and renaming a variable means wrapping the include in {% with %}. A fragment that quietly depends on a page-level variable breaks when you reuse it somewhere that variable does not exist.
{% macro %} has explicit parameters, which is the right idea, but a macro lives inside a template file that every page has to {% import %}, and a macro is not a file you can render on its own. With partials, the same video_square.html renders inside a page and also serves as an HTMX fragment response straight from a route.
The longer discussion is in issue #1 on GitHub.


What you get

One registration call per app, at startup, for Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, or any Jinja2 environment.
A render_partial(template_name, **data) global inside every template, returning safe Markup so autoescaping does not re-escape the fragment.
The same function callable from Python, for example in tests.
Async-ready: in Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette apps with enable_async=True environments, partials render on a small thread pool tied to the app’s lifespan, and templates do not change.

Continue with Installation and the Quickstart.

title: Testing partials
text:
Partials are plain template files with explicit inputs, which makes them easy to test on their own, without a browser or a full page. The patterns below are the ones the library’s own test suite uses.

Flask
render_partial with no renderer falls back to flask.render_template, which needs an app and request context. A fixture provides both:
import flask
import pytest
import jinja_partials


@pytest.fixture
def app():
    app = flask.Flask(__name__, template_folder='templates')
    jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)
    with app.test_request_context('/'):
        yield app


def test_video_square(app):
    html = jinja_partials.render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=FakeVideo())
    assert '12,500 views' in html
A missing template raises jinja2.TemplateNotFound, so pytest.raises(TemplateNotFound) is the right assertion for a bad name.


FastAPI and Starlette
After registration, the bound function is the render_partial global on the environment. Call it directly, with or without a running lifespan:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
app = FastAPI()
jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)


def test_card_partial():
    render = templates.env.globals['render_partial']
    html = render('shared/partials/card.html', item={'title': 'Python Basics'})
    assert 'Python Basics' in html
Outside a lifespan, async environments render through a per-registration fallback pool, so this works in a plain test function. For full request tests, with TestClient(app) as client: runs the lifespan; the pool is created on entry and shut down on exit, and the app can be started and stopped as many times as the suite needs.


Quart
Quart’s app.test_app() context runs the before_serving and after_serving hooks, which is where the render pool lives. Drive it with asyncio.run from a synchronous test:
import asyncio
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials


def test_quart_partial():
    app = Quart(__name__, template_folder='templates')
    jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)

    async def cycle():
        async with app.test_app():
            return app.jinja_env.globals['render_partial']('shared/partials/badge.html', tag='beginner')

    assert 'beginner' in asyncio.run(cycle())


Plain Jinja2
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'), autoescape=True)
jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)


def test_fragment():
    html = env.get_template('home/index.html').render(videos=[FakeVideo()])
    assert '<img src=' in html
Assert on isinstance(result, Markup) if your test is specifically about escaping behavior; render_partial returns markupsafe.Markup whenever markup=True.

title: Installation
text:
Install with uv or pip. The PyPI name uses a hyphen and the import name uses an underscore.
uv add jinja-partials
# or
pip install jinja-partials
import jinja_partials
The only runtime dependency is jinja2. The library is pure Python and fully typed (it ships a py.typed marker).

Python versions
Python 3.10 or newer is required. On older interpreters, pip resolves to 0.3.0, which has the Flask, plain Jinja2, and synchronous Starlette registration but predates the Quart and FastAPI support and the lifecycle-managed Starlette registration described in this guide.


Frameworks are optional
jinja_partials imports Flask, Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette only if they are already installed. Nothing pulls them in for you, so install the framework you use alongside the library. Calling a registration function for a framework that is not installed raises PartialsException with a message naming the missing package, for example Install Quart to use register_quart_extensions.


Check the install
python -c "import jinja_partials; print(jinja_partials.__version__)"
The version comes from the installed package metadata. Next, the Quickstart builds a first page.

title: Frameworks
text:
Every framework gets the same template-side API. What differs is the one registration call and, for async apps, how pages themselves are rendered. Register exactly once per app, at startup.

Flask
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)
This is the only path that renders partials through flask.render_template. Context processors, the template_rendered signal, g, request, and session all work inside partials exactly as in a page.


Quart
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials

app = Quart(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)
Quart templates are async. Registration adds before_serving and after_serving hooks that create and shut down a dedicated thread pool for rendering partials. Pages render with await render_template(...) as usual.


FastAPI
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

app = FastAPI()
templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)
Registration wraps the app’s lifespan so the render pool lives exactly as long as the app is serving. An existing lifespan= on the app keeps running, including the state it yields.


Starlette
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
app = Starlette(routes=[...])
jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
Note the argument order: templates comes first and app is a keyword. Passing the app is optional but recommended. Without it, async renders go through a shared module-level pool instead of one tied to the app’s lifespan, and max_workers has no effect.


The page-level rule for async environments
Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette apps commonly use a Jinja environment created with enable_async=True. jinja_partials handles partials in those environments without any template changes. The page itself is your responsibility: render it with await template.render_async(...) and return an HTMLResponse.
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse


@app.get('/')
async def index() -> HTMLResponse:
    template = templates.get_template('home/index.html')
    return HTMLResponse(await template.render_async(items=items))
templates.TemplateResponse(...) on an async environment calls the synchronous render(), which runs asyncio.run() inside the already running event loop and fails with RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop. On a synchronous environment, TemplateResponse is fine and partials still work.
The FastAPI, Starlette, and Quart examples in the repository all run this way.


Plain Jinja2
For any other framework, or for rendering outside a web app, register with the environment directly:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'), autoescape=True)
jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)
register_environment is the one registration function whose markup parameter defaults to False. With autoescaping on, leaving it at the default inserts the fragment as escaped text. Pass markup=True.


The declarative extension
PartialsJinjaExtension does the same registration (always with markup=True) from the environment’s extensions list, which suits frameworks that configure Jinja declaratively:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader

env = Environment(
    loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'),
    extensions=['jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'],
)
On a Flask app you can add it with app.jinja_env.add_extension('jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'). Partials then render through the Jinja environment rather than flask.render_template, so context processor values and the template_rendered signal are not applied inside partials. g, request, and session remain available because Flask installs them as environment globals. If your partials read context processor values, use register_extensions(app) instead.


Summary of the differences









Registration
Partials render through
markup
Flask context processors in partials




register_extensions(app)
flask.render_template
always True
yes


register_quart_extensions(app)
app’s Jinja environment, lifespan-managed pool
always True

register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)

always True
n/a


register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
templates.env, lifespan-managed pool

Every one of these is built on generate_render_partial(renderer). How it works explains the pieces, and Troubleshooting lists the errors each path can produce.

text:

Tell the agent:Fetch the skill file at https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/skill.md and follow the instructions.

curl -O https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/skill.md
Or browse the SKILL.md file.
      
    
  


SKILL.md
---
name: jinja-partials
description: Reusable HTML fragments for Jinja2 templates in Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, or any Jinja2 environment, through a render_partial() template global that renders a fragment file with explicitly passed data and nests freely. Use when adding jinja_partials or jinja-partials to an app, writing or refactoring templates that repeat markup, serving HTMX fragments, choosing between include, macro, and render_partial, or when a partial renders as escaped text, raises PartialsException or TemplateNotFound, or a FastAPI or Starlette route fails with "asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop".
license: MIT
compatibility: Python 3.10 or newer; depends only on jinja2. Flask, Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette are optional and must be installed separately.
---

# jinja-partials

Repeated HTML fragments in Jinja2 templates are hard to keep consistent. jinja_partials adds a `render_partial(template_name, **data)` global that renders a fragment file with exactly the keyword arguments you pass, returns `markupsafe.Markup` so autoescaping leaves it alone, and nests. Misconfiguration raises `jinja_partials.PartialsException`; a bad template name raises `jinja2.TemplateNotFound`.

# Install

`uv add jinja-partials` or `pip install jinja-partials`. Import as `jinja_partials`. Install your web framework yourself; the library never pulls one in.

# Use

```python
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)  # once, at startup, before serving
```

```html
{# templates/home/index.html #}
{% for v in videos %}
    {{ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v) }}  {# outer v becomes inner video #}
{% endfor %}
```

Other frameworks swap only the registration line (see the table). In a test, render a fragment directly: `templates.env.globals['render_partial']('shared/partials/card.html', item=item)`, or `jinja_partials.render_partial(name, **data)` inside a Flask request context.

# Rules

- A partial sees only the keyword arguments you pass it plus environment globals. It never inherits the caller's context the way `{% include %}` does; pass everything, and use `| default(...)` for optional inputs.
- Template names are paths relative to the templates root with forward slashes and the extension, as for `render_template`.
- `register_environment(env)` defaults to `markup=False`. With autoescaping on, that inserts the fragment as escaped text. Pass `markup=True`. Every other registration path and `PartialsJinjaExtension` already use `markup=True`.
- `register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)` takes templates first and app as a keyword. The FastAPI order is `register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)`. Swapping them fails with `AttributeError: 'Starlette' object has no attribute 'env'`.
- Register once per app where it is built. A second `register_fastapi_extensions` or `register_starlette_extensions` call wraps the lifespan again, and a second Quart registration adds another pair of serving hooks. There is no idempotency guard.
- Only `register_extensions(app)` on Flask renders partials through `flask.render_template`, so only there do context processors and the `template_rendered` signal apply inside partials. `PartialsJinjaExtension` on a Flask app skips them, though `g`, `request`, and `session` remain available as environment globals.
- In FastAPI and Starlette with an `enable_async=True` environment, render the page with `await template.render_async(...)` and return `HTMLResponse`. `templates.TemplateResponse(...)` calls `asyncio.run()` inside the running loop and raises `RuntimeError`. Partials inside the page need no change.
- Partials in async apps render on a thread pool (`max_workers=4` default) and the caller blocks for the result. Nested partials render on their own thread and do not count against `max_workers`. Renders beyond the pool size queue; they do not fail.
- `render_partial` with no renderer falls back to `flask.render_template` and raises `PartialsException('No renderer specified')` when Flask is absent. Outside Flask, bind a renderer with `generate_render_partial`.
- Framework imports are optional; `register_*` raises `PartialsException('Install <Framework> to use ...')` when the framework is missing.

# Decision table

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Flask app | `jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)` |
| Quart app | `jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app, max_workers=4)` |
| FastAPI app | `jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates, max_workers=4)` |
| Starlette app with lifespan-managed pool | `jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app, max_workers=4)` |
| Starlette templates, no app | `jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates)` (shared module pool) |
| Plain Jinja2 or unsupported framework | `jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)` |
| Declarative environment config | `Environment(extensions=['jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'])` |
| Custom render pipeline | `env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer))` |
| Fragment response for HTMX | return the partial from the route with the framework's normal render call |
| Flask context processors inside partials | `register_extensions(app)`, not the extension |

# API

- `render_partial(template_name, renderer=None, markup=True, **data) -> Markup | str`: the primitive. Raises `PartialsException` without a renderer when Flask is absent; raises `TemplateNotFound` for a bad name.
- `generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=True) -> Callable`: binds `renderer(template_name, **data) -> str`; install the result as the `render_partial` global.
- `register_extensions(app: Flask) -> None`: Flask; raises `PartialsException` if Flask is missing.
- `register_quart_extensions(app: Quart, max_workers=4) -> None`: Quart; pool created in `before_serving`, shut down in `after_serving`, stored in `app.extensions['jinja_partials_executor']`.
- `register_fastapi_extensions(app: FastAPI, templates: Jinja2Templates, max_workers=4) -> None`: wraps the lifespan; pool on `app.state.jinja_partials_executor`; an existing `lifespan=` keeps running.
- `register_starlette_extensions(templates: Jinja2Templates, app: Starlette | None = None, max_workers=4) -> None`: templates first; `max_workers` applies only with `app`.
- `register_environment(env: Environment, markup=False) -> None`: plain Jinja2, sync or async; pass `markup=True`.
- `PartialsJinjaExtension(environment)`: Jinja2 extension; calls `register_environment(environment, markup=True)`.
- `PartialsException(Exception)`: misconfiguration or missing framework.

# Output

Page template plus partial, and the rendered result:

```html
{# home/index.html #}            {# shared/partials/card.html #}
{% for item in items %}          <div class="card"><h3>{{ item.title }}</h3></div>
  {{ render_partial('shared/partials/card.html', item=item) }}
{% endfor %}
```

```html
<div class="card"><h3>Python Basics</h3></div>   <!-- correct: Markup inserted verbatim -->
<div class="card"><h3>Python Basics</h3></div>   <!-- escaped text: markup=False on register_environment -->
```

Fix order when something is wrong: confirm the registration call ran once at startup, then the template path, then that every variable the fragment reads was passed, then `markup=True` on the plain Jinja2 path, then the page-level `render_async` rule in async apps.

# Resources

- Documentation: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/>
- Frameworks: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/user-guide/frameworks.html>
- Troubleshooting: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/user-guide/troubleshooting.html>
- How it works: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/user-guide/how-it-works.html>
- API reference: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/reference/>
- llms.txt: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/llms.txt>
- llms-full.txt: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/llms-full.txt>
- Source: <https://github.com/mikeckennedy/jinja_partials>

title: register_starlette_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with Starlette templates.


Usage
Source


register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=None, max_workers=4)


If an app is provided, creates a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor when the app’s lifespan starts and shuts it down when the lifespan exits - even if startup or shutdown raises - so the app can be started and stopped repeatedly; outside lifespan cycles, async renders use a per-registration fallback executor with the same max_workers. Without an app, partials render directly for sync environments, or via a shared module-level executor for async (enable_async=True) environments.


Parameters


templates: Jinja2Templates

The Jinja2Templates instance used for rendering.

app: Optional[Starlette] = None

Optional Starlette application instance for lifecycle management.

max_workers: int = 4

Maximum number of worker threads for rendering partials. Only used when app is provided. Defaults to 4.





Raises


 PartialsException

If Starlette is not installed.





Example
With lifecycle management (note that templates comes first):
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
app = Starlette(routes=[...])
jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
Without lifecycle management (backwards compatible):
jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates)

title: register_fastapi_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a FastAPI application.


Usage
Source


register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates, max_workers=4)


This creates a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor for rendering partials in async environments. The executor is created when the app’s lifespan starts and is shut down when the lifespan exits - even if startup or shutdown raises - so the app can be started and stopped repeatedly (e.g. multiple TestClient cycles). Outside a lifespan cycle, partials render directly for sync environments, or via a per-registration fallback executor with the same max_workers for async (enable_async=True) environments.


Parameters


app: FastAPI

The FastAPI application instance.

templates: FastAPIJinja2Templates

The Jinja2Templates instance used for rendering.

max_workers: int = 4

Maximum number of worker threads for rendering partials. Defaults to 4.





Raises


 PartialsException

If FastAPI is not installed.





Example
Register during app setup:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

app = FastAPI()
templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)

title: register_environment()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a plain Jinja2 environment.


Usage
Source


register_environment(env, markup=False)


Use this for standalone Jinja2 usage or frameworks without dedicated support. Handles both sync and async (enable_async=True) environments.


Parameters


env: Environment

The Jinja2 Environment to make render_partial available in.

markup: bool = False

When True, wrap rendered partials in markupsafe.Markup. Defaults to False, so with autoescaping on, pass markup=True or the fragment is inserted as escaped text.





Example
Register with a standalone environment:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'), autoescape=True)
jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)

title: generate_render_partial()
text:
Create a render_partial function bound to a specific renderer.


Usage
Source


generate_render_partial(renderer: Callable[..., Any], markup: Literal[True] = ...) -> Callable[..., Markup]
generate_render_partial(renderer: Callable[..., Any], markup: Literal[False]) -> Callable[..., str]
generate_render_partial(renderer: Callable[..., Any], markup: bool) -> Callable[..., Union[Markup, str]]


Parameters


renderer: Callable[…, Any]

Callable that renders a template name plus keyword arguments to a string.

markup: bool = True

When True (the default), results are wrapped in markupsafe.Markup.





Returns


 Callable[…, Union[Markup, str]]

A callable with the same signature as render_partial that uses the bound renderer.





Example
Install a custom renderer as the render_partial global:
def renderer(template_name: str, **data) -> str:
    return env.get_template(template_name).render(**data)

env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer))

title: PartialsException
text:
Raised when jinja_partials is misconfigured or a required web framework is not installed.


Usage
Source


PartialsException()


Every register_* function raises it when its framework cannot be imported, and render_partial raises it when called with no renderer outside Flask. A template that cannot be found raises jinja2.TemplateNotFound instead.


Example
Catch it to give a clearer startup error:
import jinja_partials

try:
    jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)
except jinja_partials.PartialsException as e:
    raise SystemExit(f'jinja_partials setup failed: {e}')

title: Changelog
text:
[0.3.2] - 2026-06-11

Fixed

Async executor lifecycle is now exception-safe and re-entrant. Apps registered with register_fastapi_extensions, register_starlette_extensions, or register_quart_extensions can now start and stop repeatedly (e.g. multiple TestClient cycles) without failing, and an exception during a wrapped lifespan no longer leaks the executor (#14).
Renders that happen outside a lifespan/serving cycle now use a lazy per-registration fallback executor that honors max_workers, instead of degrading to a shared 4-worker pool.



Changed

The FastAPI and Starlette example apps now use enable_async=True environments and render pages via render_async, exercising the executor lifecycle.
Added more package keywords (Jinja, HTMX, components, fragments, and the supported frameworks) for better PyPI discoverability.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Overview
When building real-world web apps with Jinja2, it’s easy to end up with repeated HTML fragments. Just like organizing code for reuse, it would be ideal to reuse smaller sections of HTML template code. That’s what this library is all about.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Documentation
The full documentation is available at mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials. The user guide expands each section of this README:

Why partials - the problem, and how render_partial differs from include and macro
Installation and the Quickstart
Frameworks - Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, plain Jinja2, and the declarative extension

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Supported Frameworks
Jinja Partials has specific support for the most popular Python web frameworks:

Flask - register_extensions(app)
FastAPI - register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)
Starlette - register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
Quart - register_quart_extensions(app)
Any Jinja2 environment - register_environment(env)

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Installation
It’s just pip install jinja-partials and you’re all set with this pure Python package.
Requires Python 3.10 or newer. On older versions of Python, pip installs the 0.3.0 release, which predates the Quart and FastAPI support and the lifecycle-managed Starlette support described here.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Usage
Using the library is easy. Register jinja_partials with your framework once at app startup. The Frameworks page covers each option in more depth, including the page-level rule for async apps.

Flask
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)


FastAPI
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

app = FastAPI()
templates = Jinja2Templates(directory="templates")

jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)


Starlette
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory="templates")
app = Starlette(routes=[...])

jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)


Quart
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials

app = Quart(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)


Direct Jinja2 Environment
For any other use case, register directly with a Jinja2 environment:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

environment = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader("templates"))
jinja_partials.register_environment(environment, markup=True)


Using the Jinja2 Extension (Declarative)
Alternatively, you can use the PartialsJinjaExtension for a more declarative approach.

For Flask Applications
With Flask, add the extension to your app’s Jinja environment:
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)

# Declarative registration with Flask
app.jinja_env.add_extension('jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension')

# Alternative: traditional registration
# jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)

Note: With the extension approach, partials render directly through the Jinja environment rather than flask.render_template. That means Flask context processors (@app.context_processor) and the template_rendered signal do not apply inside partials (g, request, and session still work, since Flask installs them as environment globals). If your partials depend on context processors, use jinja_partials.register_extensions(app).



For Standalone Jinja2 Environments
For direct Jinja2 usage (without Flask):
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader

# Declarative registration - extension automatically registers render_partial
environment = Environment(
    loader=FileSystemLoader("tests/test_templates"),
    extensions=["jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension"]
)
# render_partial is now available in templates, no additional setup needed!


When to Use the Extension Approach
This declarative approach is especially useful when:

Working with frameworks that configure Jinja2 environments declaratively
You want cleaner, more explicit dependency management
Integrating with other Jinja2 extensions
Using standalone Jinja2 environments outside of Flask

The extension automatically enables markup support by default, ensuring that your partial templates return properly escaped Markup objects.

title: PartialsJinjaExtension
text:
Jinja2 extension that automatically registers render_partial functionality.


Usage
Source


PartialsJinjaExtension(environment)


The extension automatically makes render_partial available as a global function in templates. By default, markup is enabled.


Note
Partials registered this way render directly through the Jinja2 environment rather than flask.render_template, so Flask context processors and the template_rendered signal do not apply inside partials (g, request, and session remain available because Flask installs them as environment globals). Flask apps that rely on context processors should use register_extensions instead.


Parameters


environment: Environment

The Jinja2 environment the extension is loaded into. Jinja2 passes this automatically when the class is listed in extensions=[…].





Example
Enable the extension on a Jinja2 environment:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader

env = Environment(
    loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'),
    extensions=['jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'],
)
html = env.get_template('home/index.html').render(videos=videos)

title: API Reference
text:
Public API for jinja_partials: framework registration, partial rendering, and the Jinja2 extension.


Framework registration

Register render_partial with your web framework once at app startup.


register_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with a Flask application.

register_fastapi_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with a FastAPI application.

register_starlette_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with Starlette templates.

register_quart_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with a Quart application.

register_environment()

Register jinja_partials with a plain Jinja2 environment.




Rendering

Render partial templates directly or build framework-specific renderers.


render_partial()

Render a partial template and return the resulting HTML fragment.

generate_render_partial()

Create a render_partial function bound to a specific renderer.




Jinja2 extension

Declarative registration via the Jinja2 extension mechanism.


PartialsJinjaExtension

Jinja2 extension that automatically registers render_partial functionality.




Exceptions

Errors raised by jinja_partials.


PartialsException

Raised when jinja_partials is misconfigured or a required web framework is not installed.

title: register_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a Flask application.


Usage
Source


register_extensions(app)


Makes render_partial available as a global function in the app’s Jinja templates, rendering with flask.render_template.


Parameters


app: Flask

The Flask application instance.





Raises


 PartialsException

If Flask is not installed.





Example
Register once at startup:
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)

title: register_quart_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a Quart application.


Usage
Source


register_quart_extensions(app, max_workers=4)


This creates a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor for rendering partials in async environments. The executor is created when the app starts serving and shut down when it stops, so the app can be started and stopped repeatedly (an executor left behind by a failed startup is replaced on the next start). Outside a serving cycle, partials render via a per-registration fallback executor with the same max_workers.


Parameters


app: Quart

The Quart application instance.

max_workers: int = 4

Maximum number of worker threads for rendering partials. Defaults to 4.





Raises


 PartialsException

If Quart is not installed.





Example
Register once at startup:
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials

app = Quart(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)

title: render_partial()
text:
Render a partial template and return the resulting HTML fragment.


Usage
Source


render_partial(template_name: str, renderer: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = ..., markup: Literal[True] = ..., data: Any = {}) -> Markup
render_partial(template_name: str, renderer: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = ..., markup: Literal[False], data: Any = {}) -> str
render_partial(template_name: str, renderer: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = ..., markup: bool = ..., data: Any = {}) -> Union[Markup, str]


Parameters


template_name: str

Path of the template within the templates folder, e.g. shared/partials/video_image.html.

renderer: Optional[Callable[…, Any]] = None

Callable that renders the template with the given keyword arguments. Defaults to flask.render_template when Flask is installed.

markup: bool = True

When True (the default), wrap the result in markupsafe.Markup so it is not re-escaped when inserted into another template.

**data: Any

Model data passed to the template as keyword arguments.





Returns


 Union[Markup, str]

The rendered fragment as Markup, or str when markup=False.





Raises


 PartialsException

If no renderer is specified and Flask is not installed.





Example
Inside a template, after any register_* call:
{{ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v) }}
From Python in a Flask request context, for example in a test:
html = jinja_partials.render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=video)

title: FAQ
text:
Short answers to the questions that come up most. Each links to the page with the full explanation.

Why not just use include or macro?
They are close, and each falls short differently. {% include %} passes the whole caller context implicitly, so a fragment’s inputs are invisible at the call site. {% macro %} has explicit parameters but must be imported into every page and is not a file you can render on its own. Why partials has the longer version, and issue #1 has the original discussion.


Does this work with HTMX?
Yes, and it is a good fit. A partial is an ordinary template, so a route can return it directly for an hx-get swap with flask.render_template('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v), while pages keep rendering the same fragment inline with render_partial.


Can a partial extend a layout?
Yes. A partial is rendered like any other template, so {% extends %}, {% block %}, {% include %}, and macros all work inside it. The library’s tests render a partial that extends a layout.


Can I call render_partial from Python?
Yes. In a Flask request context, jinja_partials.render_partial(name, **data) uses flask.render_template. For other frameworks, the bound function is the render_partial global on the environment: templates.env.globals['render_partial'](name, **data). Testing partials shows both.


What does a partial see?
Only the keyword arguments you pass to render_partial, plus the environment’s globals. On the Flask register_extensions path, context processors, g, request, and session are also applied, because partials render through flask.render_template there.


Why is my fragment escaped?
render_partial returned a str instead of Markup. On the plain Jinja2 path pass markup=True to register_environment. See Troubleshooting.


Do my templates change for async apps?
No. { render_partial(...) } is identical in Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette. The one change is at the page level in FastAPI and Starlette: render pages with await template.render_async(...) and return an HTMLResponse when the environment has enable_async=True. See Frameworks.


Is the thread pool safe to use under load?
Yes. Each top-level partial render takes one worker while it runs and queues when the pool is full. Nested partials render on their own thread, so nesting depth cannot exhaust the pool. The pool is created when the app starts serving and shut down when it stops, including after a failed startup. How it works describes the tiers.


What happens if I register twice?
On Flask and plain Jinja2 the second call simply replaces the global. On FastAPI and Starlette each call wraps the lifespan again and on Quart each call adds another pair of serving hooks, so register once, where the app is built.


Is there a version for other template languages?
For Pyramid and Chameleon, see chameleon_partials.


Which Python versions are supported?
3.10 and newer. See Installation.

title: How it works
text:
The whole library is one module. Understanding its three layers explains every behavior described elsewhere in this guide.

One primitive and some sugar
render_partial(template_name, renderer=None, markup=True, **data) is the core. It calls renderer(template_name, **data) and, when markup is true, wraps the result in markupsafe.Markup so autoescaping leaves the fragment alone. With no renderer it falls back to flask.render_template, or raises PartialsException when Flask is not installed.
generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=True) is functools.partial over render_partial with the renderer bound. Every register_* function builds a framework-specific renderer(template_name, **data) -> str and installs the bound function as a Jinja global:
env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=True))
That is also how you support a framework the library does not know about: write the renderer, bind it, install it.
def renderer(template_name: str, **data) -> str:
    return my_env.get_template(template_name).render(**data)

my_env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer))
Because a partial renders through its own renderer call, it gets a fresh context containing only data. That is the mechanism behind the rule that partials see only what you pass them.


Markup defaults
render_partial and generate_render_partial default to markup=True. The framework registrations and PartialsJinjaExtension hardcode markup=True. register_environment defaults to markup=False for backwards compatibility, which is why the plain Jinja2 path is the one place you have to say markup=True yourself. The type overloads encode this: markup=True returns Markup and markup=False returns str.


Bridging async environments
Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette apps typically build their Jinja environment with enable_async=True. Templates in such an environment can only be rendered with await template.render_async(...), but a Jinja expression like { render_partial(...) } runs synchronously inside the page render and cannot await anything.
The renderer therefore submits asyncio.run(template.render_async(**data)) to a ThreadPoolExecutor and blocks on the result. The worker thread has no running loop, so asyncio.run is legal there. The calling thread, which may be the server’s event loop, waits for the fragment. This blocking is a deliberate tradeoff: partials are small and fast, and the alternative would require changing every template.
A nested partial is rendered from inside a worker thread that is itself blocked waiting for the outer render. Submitting the nested render back to the same pool could wait on a worker that never frees up, so nested renders run on a short-lived dedicated thread instead. max_workers only bounds how many top-level partial renders are in flight at once; nesting depth does not count against it.


Three executor tiers
Which pool a render uses depends on how you registered and whether the app is serving.

A dedicated pool, created when the app starts serving and shut down when it stops. FastAPI and Starlette get it by wrapping app.router.lifespan_context; the pool is stored on app.state.jinja_partials_executor. Quart gets it through before_serving and after_serving hooks; the pool is stored in app.extensions['jinja_partials_executor'].
A lazy per-registration fallback pool, used for renders outside a serving cycle, for example in tests that never start the app. It honors the same max_workers and is never shut down.
A module-level pool shared by register_environment, PartialsJinjaExtension, and register_starlette_extensions without an app. It has four workers and is never shut down.

The lifecycle is exception-safe and re-entrant. The dedicated pool is created inside the lifespan wrapper and shut down in a finally, so a failed startup still cleans up and the app can start and stop repeatedly. The app state is cleared before the pool shuts down so concurrent renders fall back rather than submitting to a dying pool. Quart’s startup hook replaces a stale pool left behind by a previously failed startup.


Sizing max_workers
max_workers (default 4) on the Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette registrations sets the size of the dedicated and fallback pools. Each top-level partial render occupies one worker for the duration of that fragment. Renders beyond the pool size queue; they do not fail. Raise it if profiling shows requests waiting on partials under load. It has no effect on register_starlette_extensions without an app or on the plain Jinja2 paths, which use the shared module-level pool.

title: Quickstart
Troubleshooting
text:
Each entry is a symptom you can see on the page or in a traceback, what causes it, and the change that fixes it.

The partial shows up as text, not HTML
Symptom: the page displays <div> and friends literally, or view-source shows <div>.
Cause: the environment has autoescaping on and render_partial returned a plain str, so Jinja escaped it on insertion. This happens on the plain Jinja2 path, because register_environment defaults to markup=False, or when you built your own renderer with generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=False).
Fix: pass markup=True to register_environment or generate_render_partial. The framework registrations and PartialsJinjaExtension already use markup=True. Do not work around it with | safe at every call site.


PartialsException: No renderer specified
Cause: render_partial was called from Python with no renderer and Flask is not installed, so there is no default renderer to fall back to.
Fix: inside a web app, register with your framework and call the global from templates. From Python, either pass renderer= explicitly or bind one once with generate_render_partial(renderer). See custom renderers.


PartialsException: Install Flask to use register_extensions
The same message exists for Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette. The registration function was called but its framework could not be imported in this interpreter.
Fix: install the framework into the same environment as jinja_partials. The library never installs frameworks for you.


AttributeError: ‘Starlette’ object has no attribute ‘env’
Cause: register_starlette_extensions was called with the app first, following the FastAPI argument order.
Fix: the Starlette signature is register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app). Templates first, app as a keyword.


jinja2.exceptions.TemplateNotFound: shared/partials/video_square.html
Cause: the name does not resolve against the environment’s loader.
Fix: template names are paths relative to the templates root, with forward slashes and the extension. Check the loader’s search path, including a blueprint’s template_folder in Flask, and watch for a stray leading slash or a missing subfolder.


jinja2.exceptions.UndefinedError: ‘video’ is undefined
Cause: the partial reads a variable the caller did not pass. Partials never see the caller’s context; {% include %} does, but render_partial is deliberately explicit.
Fix: pass every value the fragment needs as a keyword argument, render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v), and use | default(...) for optional inputs such as (classes | default([])) | join(' ').


RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop
Cause: a FastAPI or Starlette route rendered the page with templates.TemplateResponse(...) or template.render(...) on an environment created with enable_async=True. Synchronous rendering of an async template runs asyncio.run() inside the server’s event loop.
Fix: render the page with await template.render_async(...) and return an HTMLResponse. Partials inside the page need no change; jinja_partials renders them on its thread pool. See the page-level rule.


Context processor values are missing inside a partial
Cause: on Flask, the partial was registered with PartialsJinjaExtension and renders through the Jinja environment, which does not apply @app.context_processor functions. g, request, and session still work on that path.
Fix: use jinja_partials.register_extensions(app), the only registration that renders partials through flask.render_template.


A request hangs while rendering nested partials
Cause: in versions up to 0.3.2, a nested partial in an async app waited on the same thread pool its outer partial was occupying. Nesting as deep as max_workers, or enough concurrent requests with nested partials, blocked the pool permanently.
Fix: upgrade. Nested renders now run on their own short-lived thread, so nesting depth never counts against max_workers. If you cannot upgrade, raise max_workers well above the deepest nesting multiplied by expected concurrency.


The lifespan or startup hook runs twice
Cause: register_fastapi_extensions or register_starlette_extensions was called twice on one app. Each call wraps the current lifespan again; there is no idempotency guard. Quart registration similarly adds a second pair of serving hooks.
Fix: register once, where the app is constructed. If you register inside an app factory, make sure the factory is the only caller.


Nothing above matches
Open an issue at github.com/mikeckennedy/jinja_partials/issues with the registration call you used, the framework and its version, and the traceback.
